source.title: More is Better in Modern Machine Learning: when Infinite Overparameterization is Optimal and Overfitting is Obligatory
source.authors: James B. Simon; Dhruva Karkada; Nikhil Ghosh; Mikhail Belkin

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices. Some figure text is garbled, but the main prose and figure captions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether increasing feature count improves test error in random-feature regression and whether near-interpolation is optimal in kernel ridge regression. These are conceptual tests of model-size/generalization and train–test-gap claims, using different models and measures from the mapped versions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test fitting random labels, compare adaptive optimizers, batch sizes, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Figure-only curves and prose-level findings are recorded where the captions or text state the outcome; no values are read from garbled plots.
record.test_reason: The study bears on V2 through width sweeps in shallow random-ReLU networks and, more directly, Appendix F.2's result that zero-ridge random-feature test risk decreases as feature count increases beyond k=n. Only output weights are trained; this differs from training both layers in V2's original setting. Kernel fitting-ratio experiments do not test any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusions. More precisely, monotonic benefits of features and samples are proved for their RF risk estimate under optimal ridge, relying on Gaussian universality and an approximate eigenframework whose derivation is nonrigorous. They also establish conditions for obligatory near-interpolation in power-law kernel tasks and report supporting convolutional-NTK experiments; added label noise raises the optimal fitting ratio.
record.recipe_differences: Random-feature regression with an optimally selected ridge parameter and kernel ridge regression with convolutional NTKs; the mapped sources concern other architectures and training recipes. The image-kernel experiments use one-hot regression and added Gaussian label noise.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimal fitting ratio changes with added label noise: it is approximately zero without added noise and becomes nonzero as noise is added. Feature-count monotonicity is stated for optimally tuned ridge.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing Gaussian random-projection feature count improves test MSE at optimally tuned ridge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More random linear features improve optimally regularized random-projection regression in the tested synthetic setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Near-interpolation minimizes convolutional-kernel regression test MSE without added noise; added label noise increases the optimal fitting ratio.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested Myrtle convolutional NTK vision tasks, optimal kernel regularization depends on label noise, with near-interpolation optimal without added noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Predicted kernel-regression errors agree with measurements after fitting an overall multiplicative prefactor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured power-law exponents predict the shape of train/test error curves across regularization and noise settings for the tested kernels.

record.problems: The RF eigenframework derivation is described by the authors as nonrigorous. The experiments test random-feature and kernel regression rather than the specified fully trained networks. For the image-task experiments, the theory curves are vertically shifted by a fitted multiplicative prefactor; the paper says agreement at zero fitting ratio is therefore obtained by construction. Exact figure values are not recoverable from the supplied flattened/garbled figure text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results left out. The paper includes theoretical results and cited prior-work comparisons; cited results are not recorded as study rows.

untested.parts: Natural-label generalization alongside near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels using the same architecture and recipe.

Training both network layers with gradient methods without explicit regularization; classification test error on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10. R1 uses optimally tuned ridge and does not itself establish interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, and transferred initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbations and their ranking of generalization gaps.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Proposition 2 gives the directly relevant zero-ridge result: for k>n, test risk is nonincreasing with feature count. It follows from Equation 54 because the feature-dependent prefactor decreases. The record's blanket exclusion of theoretical results omits an argument bearing directly on V2.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Remove the record's limits_scope verdict: using a different recipe and leaving original settings untested do not demonstrate a failure or limitation of V2. Exact plotted MSE values cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.

The specified one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained to convergence without explicit regularization on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10; zero training error and behavior specifically beyond the width needed to fit.
Convolutional versus fully connected network comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance.
Large-batch training and its dependence on epoch budget or recipe.
Dropout and its interaction with training-set size or data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.note: Caption states that at optimal ridge more features monotonically improve test performance. The experiment is random-feature regression; the plotted numeric values are not recoverable from the supplied figure text.
rows.check: Figure 1 explicitly reports decreasing test MSE with feature count at optimal ridge. Identify the measure as regression MSE and the network as having frozen random hidden weights. This row alone does not establish zero training error or the unregularized width result.
